pack-digital-backpack.name: Pack Your Digital Backpack
pack-digital-backpack.description: Decide what information goes in your school backpack — and what stays home. Then practice the same idea for the internet!
pack-digital-backpack.realLifeScenario: You want to join a fun online game. It asks for your name, school, and home address. What should you share?
pack-digital-backpack.learningObjective: Help younger children tell the difference between friendly facts and private details.
pack-digital-backpack.familyPrompt: Create a “share / ask first / keep private” list together using examples from your child’s favourite apps or games.
pack-digital-backpack.nextStep: Do a one-minute check of one favourite app and spot the questions it asks before sign-up.
keyLearnings: Your home address and full name are private — keep them at home
A nickname or first name only is fine for games
Ask a grown-up before filling in any forms online
discussionPrompts: Which backpack items feel safe to carry online, and which stay at home?
Who in our family can help you decide before you share something new?

traffic-light-safety.name: Traffic Light: Safe or Not?
traffic-light-safety.description: Use a red, yellow, and green light to decide if sharing something online is safe, risky, or definitely not okay.
traffic-light-safety.realLifeScenario: A fun game says: “You won a prize! Tell us your address to receive it.” Red, yellow, or green?
traffic-light-safety.learningObjective: Build a simple family language for stop, slow down, and ask for help online.
traffic-light-safety.familyPrompt: Pick three real examples from games, videos, or chat messages and decide together whether they are red, yellow, or green.
traffic-light-safety.nextStep: Place a traffic-light reminder near the family device you use most often.
keyLearnings: Green = safe to share (favourite colour, pet name)
Yellow = ask a grown-up first (your photo, school name)
Red = never share online (address, phone number, password)
discussionPrompts: What clues tell you a message should be red instead of green?
What should our family do when something feels yellow and confusing?

secret-keeper-club.name: Secret Keeper Club
secret-keeper-club.description: Privacy Panda's treasure chest needs a special password only family knows. Learn why passwords keep our secrets safe!
secret-keeper-club.realLifeScenario: Your best friend asks for your tablet password so they can show you something cool. What should you do?
secret-keeper-club.learningObjective: Introduce passwords as family-only secrets that protect trusted spaces and devices.
secret-keeper-club.familyPrompt: Invent a silly passphrase together and practise how to keep it secret when someone is watching.
secret-keeper-club.nextStep: Review one child account together and check whether the password still feels strong and private.
keyLearnings: Passwords are like house keys — only for your family
A good password is long and uses letters, numbers, and a symbol
Never type your password where others can see
discussionPrompts: Why does a password need to stay private even from friends?
What helps you remember a strong password without saying it out loud?

trusted-adults-online.name: Who Can I Talk To Online?
trusted-adults-online.description: Sort online contacts into trusted family, known adults, and strangers — and learn when to ask a grown-up for help.
trusted-adults-online.realLifeScenario: While playing a game, someone you do not know sends you a message asking where you live. What do you do?
trusted-adults-online.learningObjective: Help children recognise when online contacts are trusted helpers and when they are strangers.
trusted-adults-online.familyPrompt: Create a short “safe grown-ups” list and rehearse who your child can go to if an online message feels uncomfortable.
trusted-adults-online.nextStep: Save your child’s trusted grown-up list somewhere they can find quickly.
keyLearnings: Online friends are still strangers until a trusted adult has checked
It is always okay to say “I need to ask my parent” and log off
Tell a trusted adult straight away if a message makes you uncomfortable
discussionPrompts: How can we tell the difference between someone we know and someone we only know online?
What words can you use when you want to pause and ask for help?

my-info-collage.name: My Public & Private Collage
my-info-collage.description: Create a collage that separates “okay to share” information from “keep private” information using Privacy Panda characters.
my-info-collage.realLifeScenario: Your class is making a school website. Which things about yourself can you put on it for everyone to see?
my-info-collage.learningObjective: Show that every post or profile shares pieces of a child’s digital footprint.
my-info-collage.familyPrompt: Build the collage with your child and let them explain why each item belongs in the public or private side.
my-info-collage.nextStep: Look at a family profile together and spot one detail you would keep private in the future.
keyLearnings: Public: hobbies, favourite food, what you like to draw
Private: your address, phone, password, or full birthday
Even friends should not share your private details for you
discussionPrompts: Which collage items would still feel safe to share with people you do not know?
How could a private detail spread if one friend posts it for you?

permission-please.name: Permission Please!
permission-please.description: Practice asking for and giving permission before sharing a photo or video of yourself or a friend online.
permission-please.realLifeScenario: Your mum takes a lovely photo of you and your friend at the park. She wants to post it. Should she ask your friend first?
permission-please.learningObjective: Teach children that privacy includes asking before posting pictures, videos, or messages.
permission-please.familyPrompt: Role-play asking permission before posting a picture from a family day out, then practise how to respond kindly to “no.”
permission-please.nextStep: Choose one family sharing rule for photos and put it somewhere everyone can see.
keyLearnings: Always ask before sharing someone else's photo
It is okay to say “no” and that choice must be respected
Once posted online, photos are very hard to remove completely
discussionPrompts: How does it feel when someone asks before posting a picture of you?
What should happen if one person says yes and another says no?

digital-footprint-trail.name: Digital Footprint Trail
digital-footprint-trail.description: Trace exactly what data Roblox, YouTube, and popular games collect about you — and decide if you are comfortable with it.
digital-footprint-trail.realLifeScenario: You have played Roblox every day for two years. What does Roblox probably know about you by now?
digital-footprint-trail.learningObjective: Help children recognise that apps build profiles from the information they collect over time.
digital-footprint-trail.familyPrompt: Pick one favourite app together and list what it probably knows about each family member who uses it.
digital-footprint-trail.nextStep: Open the privacy settings for one app you use often and review the data controls together.
keyLearnings: Games and apps track your location, search history, and play patterns
This data can be sold to other companies
Checking privacy settings regularly helps limit what is collected
discussionPrompts: Which bits of data would surprise you if an app collected them about our family?
What is the difference between fun game data and information that feels too personal?

phishing-patrol.name: Phishing Patrol
phishing-patrol.description: Spot fake messages pretending to be from games, schools, or prize competitions. Real-style examples in a safe practice space.
phishing-patrol.realLifeScenario: “You won 10,000 Robux! Click here and log in to claim your reward.” Is this message real or a trick?
phishing-patrol.learningObjective: Teach families to slow down, check the sender, and avoid urgent scam messages.
phishing-patrol.familyPrompt: Share two fake-message examples and have your child point out the scam clues before you reveal the answer.
phishing-patrol.nextStep: Practise opening a trusted website directly instead of using a message link.
keyLearnings: Phishing messages create urgency and promise rewards
Check the sender address — it is often slightly wrong
Never click links in messages; go directly to the official website
discussionPrompts: What words in a message are trying to rush you before you think?
What is our family rule when a message asks us to click a login link?

app-permission-inspector.name: App Permission Inspector
app-permission-inspector.description: Investigate why apps request camera, location, and contacts — and decide which permissions are necessary vs. suspicious.
app-permission-inspector.realLifeScenario: A new game asks for access to your location, contacts, and microphone. Should you allow all of these?
app-permission-inspector.learningObjective: Help children question whether an app really needs the data or device access it requests.
app-permission-inspector.familyPrompt: Review one installed app together and vote on which permissions are essential, optional, or unnecessary.
app-permission-inspector.nextStep: Audit one child-safe app together and turn off at least one permission you do not need.
keyLearnings: A torch app never needs your contacts — that is a red flag
Location should only be enabled when the app actually needs it
You can change app permissions at any time in your phone settings
discussionPrompts: Which permission would you challenge first, and why?
How can we decide whether an app request is useful or excessive?

privacy-settings-pro.name: Privacy Settings Pro
privacy-settings-pro.description: Practice configuring privacy settings in simulated Instagram and Roblox accounts to protect your profile from strangers.
privacy-settings-pro.realLifeScenario: Your parent just allowed you to create an Instagram account. Walk through making it private and safe, step by step.
privacy-settings-pro.learningObjective: Build confidence changing privacy settings before a child starts a new social or gaming account.
privacy-settings-pro.familyPrompt: Use this activity as a family setup checklist before your child joins a new platform.
privacy-settings-pro.nextStep: Schedule a monthly ten-minute privacy-settings review for the apps your child uses most.
keyLearnings: Set your account to Private so only approved followers see your posts
Turn off “Show activity status” to avoid telling strangers when you are online
Never share your phone number on a public profile
discussionPrompts: Which settings feel most important before posting your first picture or video?
How often should we review privacy settings together after an app update?

screenshot-safety.name: Screenshot Safety Challenge
screenshot-safety.description: Learn what happens when screenshots are shared and practise the decision of whether to send or stop before you forward anything.
screenshot-safety.realLifeScenario: A classmate messages you a funny screenshot of another friend looking silly. They want you to share it in the class group chat.
screenshot-safety.learningObjective: Show how screenshots can turn private moments into lasting digital footprints.
screenshot-safety.familyPrompt: Talk through a real group-chat situation and decide together when forwarding a screenshot would cross a line.
screenshot-safety.nextStep: Create a family pause phrase for chats: “Would I share this if everyone could see it?”
keyLearnings: Screenshots can spread far beyond the original audience
Sharing someone else's image without permission can be a form of cyberbullying
Ask: “Would I be okay if this were a screenshot of me?”
discussionPrompts: What changes when a private message becomes a screenshot?
How could you step out of a screenshot chain without making things worse?

password-strength-lab.name: Password Strength Lab
password-strength-lab.description: Test real-looking passwords and learn what makes them strong or weak. Build a memorable passphrase you will actually use.
password-strength-lab.realLifeScenario: Your school account password is “123abc”. Your IT teacher says it was found in a data breach. Create a better one now.
password-strength-lab.learningObjective: Teach families how to build strong, memorable passwords without reusing them everywhere.
password-strength-lab.familyPrompt: Challenge each other to turn weak sample passwords into stronger passphrases and explain why the new version wins.
password-strength-lab.nextStep: Choose one important family account and update it to a stronger password or passphrase.
keyLearnings: Longer passphrases (3–4 random words) beat short complex passwords
Never reuse the same password across different accounts
A password manager app can remember strong passwords for you
discussionPrompts: Why is a long phrase easier to remember and harder to crack?
Which family accounts would cause the biggest problem if their password was reused?

password-fortress-builder.name: Password Fortress Builder
password-fortress-builder.description: Build a complete personal security system: passphrases, a password manager strategy, and two-factor authentication on key accounts.
password-fortress-builder.realLifeScenario: You have 25 different online accounts. One gets hacked and you realise you used the same password everywhere. Fix this now.
password-fortress-builder.learningObjective: Help teens build a security plan they will actually keep using.
password-fortress-builder.familyPrompt: Ask your teen to map out their top three accounts and decide which one should get a stronger password or 2FA first.
password-fortress-builder.nextStep: Turn on 2FA for one important account together and save the backup codes somewhere secure.
keyLearnings: A password manager stores strong unique passwords for every account
Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) on email and social accounts
Your email account unlocks everything else—protect it most carefully
discussionPrompts: Which account would cause the most damage if it were compromised first?
What security habits feel realistic to keep every week, not just today?

online-reputation-audit.name: Online Reputation Audit
online-reputation-audit.description: See what shows up when someone searches your name online—and decide what you want to change before a job or college application.
online-reputation-audit.realLifeScenario: You are applying for a summer job. The manager searches your name before the interview. What do they find?
online-reputation-audit.learningObjective: Help teens understand that old posts can affect future opportunities.
online-reputation-audit.familyPrompt: Invite your teen to do a private “search your name” review and talk through what feels accurate, outdated, or too public.
online-reputation-audit.nextStep: Review one public-facing profile or search result and decide whether to edit, archive, or strengthen it.
keyLearnings: Search your name every few months so you know what is public
Old posts and tagged photos can still appear years later
Adding positive content (school projects, volunteering) can balance what people see
discussionPrompts: What parts of your current online footprint would you be proud to have a future employer see?
What would you want to change before an interview or university application?

data-broker-discovery.name: Data Broker Discovery
data-broker-discovery.description: Find out what data-broker websites may list about your family—and how to request removal.
data-broker-discovery.realLifeScenario: You find a website listing your home address and family members—searchable by anyone. How did it get there?
data-broker-discovery.learningObjective: Show how public records and purchases can create detailed online profiles.
data-broker-discovery.familyPrompt: Research one broker site together and decide whether your family wants to submit a removal request.
data-broker-discovery.nextStep: Pick one broker or people-search site and document the opt-out steps for later follow-up.
keyLearnings: Data brokers collect info from public records, social media, and purchases
Most broker sites have an opt-out page—it takes time but works
Paid removal services exist if you want help with many sites at once
discussionPrompts: Which personal details feel most surprising or invasive when listed by a broker?
How much effort would our family invest to remove public listings, and where would we start?

privacy-rights-challenge.name: Privacy Rights Challenge
privacy-rights-challenge.description: Learn what privacy laws mean for teens—when schools and apps need permission before sharing student data.
privacy-rights-challenge.realLifeScenario: Your school wants to share student assessment data with a tutoring app. Do they need your parents' permission first?
privacy-rights-challenge.learningObjective: Connect privacy laws to everyday school and app situations.
privacy-rights-challenge.familyPrompt: Read one privacy right together and discuss where it could matter in your teen’s school, sports, or app life.
privacy-rights-challenge.nextStep: Choose one service your teen uses and check where it explains deletion, consent, or data-access rights.
keyLearnings: US and EU laws give families rights over how children's data is used
In many places you can ask a company to delete your personal data
US schools follow FERPA—parents can review education records on request
discussionPrompts: Which privacy right would you use first if a company collected too much about you?
How should parents and teens work together when schools or apps request consent?

social-media-simulator.name: Social Media Privacy Simulator
social-media-simulator.description: Make real privacy decisions in a realistic social media simulator — posting, sharing, DMs, and location tagging — and see the consequences.
social-media-simulator.realLifeScenario: You post a photo from a party. Three days later it causes drama at school. Walk through removing it, managing reposts, and the aftermath.
social-media-simulator.learningObjective: Give teens a safe space to practise high-pressure sharing decisions before they happen for real.
social-media-simulator.familyPrompt: Use the scenario to agree on one family “pause before posting” habit that respects your teen’s independence.
social-media-simulator.nextStep: Review location-sharing settings on one social app and decide whether the default is still right for you.
keyLearnings: Location tags on photos reveal exactly where you were and when
Even deleted posts can be screenshotted and saved by others
Think before posting: “Am I happy for my grandparent, teacher, and future boss to see this?”
discussionPrompts: Which part of a post feels most risky: the caption, the photo, the location, or the audience?
How would you recover if a post reached more people than you expected?

ai-and-your-privacy.name: AI & Your Privacy
ai-and-your-privacy.description: Understand what AI tools like ChatGPT do with your prompts, and learn safe practices for using AI without accidentally exposing personal information.
ai-and-your-privacy.realLifeScenario: You paste a friend's personal essay into ChatGPT to get feedback. What are the privacy implications for your friend — and for you?
ai-and-your-privacy.learningObjective: Help teens treat AI prompts like public submissions unless they know the privacy settings and limits.
ai-and-your-privacy.familyPrompt: Talk through one real AI use case from school and decide what information is safe to include and what must stay private.
ai-and-your-privacy.nextStep: Choose one AI tool you use and review its privacy settings, history, and data controls together.
keyLearnings: AI prompts may be used to train future models — treat them like public messages
Never paste personal data (passport numbers, addresses, medical info) into AI tools
Check the privacy settings of any AI service before sharing sensitive content
discussionPrompts: What kinds of homework or personal data should stay out of an AI prompt completely?
How can you get AI help without sharing someone else’s sensitive information?

ageGroupDescriptions.5-8: Simple rules about secrets, strangers, and asking a grown-up first
ageGroupDescriptions.9-12: Spot scams, check app settings, and see what apps learn about you over time
ageGroupDescriptions.13-17: Passwords, social media, and your rights—skills teens use in real life
